title: Wendell and the Detention
premise: Ansel Sterling has perfected invisibility: flawless grades, zero opinions, a locker full of secrets she never opens. When her AP English teacher assigns the same college essay prompt to the whole class — 'Describe a moment you could not be yourself' — Ansel writes the truth for once and accidentally submits it to the school's anonymous writing contest. The essay wins, is read aloud at assembly, and detonates her carefully managed life: her debate-champion reputation, her parents' expectations, and her friendship with the one person who recognized her voice. As the school tears itself apart over who wrote it, Ansel finds an unlikely found family in detention — the misfits she spent years avoiding — and must decide whether reclaiming her name is worth losing everything she built to survive.
about_author: Ansel Sandoval is a former high-school debate coach who spent six years watching brilliant teenagers say everything except what they meant. They write in a converted garage in Portland, surrounded by trophies they never dust.

chapters.title: The Art of Being Unremarkable
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. We meet seventeen-year-old Ansel mid-debate tournament, winning on autopilot while cataloguing every rule of survival at Crestwood High: agree, achieve, disappear. At home, her mother rehearses Ansel's future like a closing argument. Beat: competent, controlled, quietly suffocating.

chapters.title: Prompt Number Four
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ms. Okafor assigns the class a shared college essay prompt — 'Describe a moment you could not be yourself' — due anonymously, best entries submitted to the school contest. Ansel drafts three safe lies, then, at 1 a.m., writes the truth about her mother's kitchen table. Beat: the first crack in the armor.

chapters.title: Submit
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A technical glitch — or fate — sends her honest draft instead of her polished one. She spends the chapter trying to recall it through the office, lying to Ms. Okafor, and nearly telling her best friend Priya. Beat: dread compounding into obsession.

chapters.title: Shortlist
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The contest shortlist posts with essays identified only by student ID numbers. Priya recognizes Ansel's rhythm in entry #4471 but says nothing, testing her own loyalty. Meanwhile the whole school speculates wildly. Beat: intimacy and betrayal braided together.

chapters.title: Assembly
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The winning essay is read aloud over the PA to eight hundred students. Ansel stands in the crowd listening to her own secret in Ms. Okafor's steady voice as classmates laugh, then go quiet. Her mother texts: 'Who wrote that? Disgusting.' Beat: public exposure, private freefall.

chapters.title: Detention, Period Nine
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Suspected by rumor if not proof, Ansel lands in Friday detention with the school's invisible kids: Theo the burnout artist, Marisol the expelled-and-reinstated, Dev the hacker who knows it was her. Nobody turns her in. Beat: unexpected warmth among the condemned.

chapters.title: The Interrogation at Dinner
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Her parents stage a formal inquiry — grades, college list, 'this essay nonsense.' Ansel deploys her debate training and loses anyway; you can't out-argue someone holding all the evidence of who you're supposed to be. Beat: the home front hardens.

chapters.title: Theo's Wall
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo shows Ansel the mural he paints illegally under the bleachers — layers of erased selves. He guesses she wrote the essay not from content but from the way she flinched at applause. Beat: being seen without being exposed.

chapters.title: Priya Draws a Line
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya confronts Ansel: 'I covered for you and you let me.' Their decade-long friendship fractures over the difference between protecting someone and erasing them. Beat: grief disguised as anger.

chapters.title: Marisol's File
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol reveals why she was expelled — she defended a bullied kid and got blamed — and shows Ansel how the school punishes honesty selectively. Ansel realizes her essay isn't just personal; it's evidence. Beat: private shame becomes political clarity.

chapters.title: Dev Offers a Delete Key
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Dev can scrub the essay from the contest archive before colleges or reporters ever see it. One keystroke and her old life resumes. Ansel asks for until Monday. Beat: temptation rendered as pure relief.

chapters.title: The Second Essay
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. In detention, Ms. Okafor quietly assigns the group an ungraded prompt: 'Who are you when no one is grading?' Ansel writes about her mother's hands, her father's silence, the self she buried to keep the peace. Beat: authorship reclaimed.

chapters.title: Leak
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Before Ansel decides, a screenshot of the essay spreads online with her name half-guessed in the comments. The choice is stolen from her — or so it seems. Dev carries the guilt of a firewall he didn't check. Beat: loss of control, rising stakes.

chapters.title: Debate Champion vs. Her Mother
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The confrontation the book has promised: at the kitchen table, Ansel finally argues for herself — not to win, but to be heard. Her mother reveals her own buried self, the life she gave up, and cannot forgive Ansel for wanting more. Beat: devastating empathy inside cruelty.

chapters.title: Walkout
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Students begin reading forbidden truths aloud in the cafeteria — Theo's art, Marisol's file, their own essays. Administration threatens suspensions. Ansel, named now whether she likes it or not, must choose to stand or hide. Beat: the movement catches fire.

chapters.title: What Priya Knew
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya admits she almost submitted Ansel's name weeks ago out of hurt. The apology is ugly and real. They rebuild on new terms: not childhood friends, but chosen ones. Beat: reconciliation without forgetting.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The school board convenes to decide Ansel's fate and the essay's removal from the archive. Ansel speaks last, using every debate skill she owns — this time for something true. Beat: climax; the argument she was born to make.

chapters.title: Verdict
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The board splits: the essay stays archived, Ansel serves a symbolic consequence, Ms. Okafor resigns in protest — a cost Ansel didn't foresee. Victory arrives wearing the price tag survival always warned her about. Beat: bittersweet triumph.

chapters.title: Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Detention continues without Ms. Okafor. The group dedicates the bleacher mural to her, painting over Theo's erased figures with faces finally visible. Ansel picks up a brush. Beat: mourning transformed into inheritance.

chapters.title: The Real Essay
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel rewrites her actual college application essay — not the safe one, not the leaked one, but the person she became between them. Her mother reads it silently, leaves it on the counter, and says nothing. Which, Ansel understands, is its own language. Beat: quiet turning point.

chapters.title: Acceptance
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Decisions arrive: one rejection from her mother's dream school, one acceptance — with a scholarship note citing 'the courage of your voice' — from a place that read the real essay. Her father, wordless, drives her to campus-visit registration himself. Beat: earned hope.

chapters.title: Head Up, Name On
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV, final day of senior year. Ansel signs the graduation program with her full name, sits with her found family — Theo, Marisol, Dev, Priya — and watches Ms. Okafor return as a guest, invited by students, not administration. She reads her essay aloud one last time, by choice, to applause she no longer flinches from. Beat: identity claimed, family chosen, survival redefined as living.
